sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: The safety of esketamine relative to other sedatives in procedural sedation remains incompletely elucidated. This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated the comparative safety of esketamine against commonly used sedative and analgesic agents across a range of respiratory, hemodynamic, and recovery outcomes.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science was conducted from 2000 to 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing esketamine with other sedatives or placebo in patients undergoing procedural sedation. Primary outcomes included respiratory events (hypoxia) and hemodynamic stability (hypotension, bradycardia, vasoactive drug use). Secondary outcomes included recovery parameters (PACU discharge time) and drug consumption. A frequentist network meta-analysis was performed, and treatments were ranked using Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) values.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Thirty-nine RCTs involving 5,885 participants were included. Esketamine demonstrated a significantly lower risk of hypoxia compared to propofol (RR 6.11, 95% CI 1.91–19.57), sufentanil (RR 2.72, 95% CI 1.48–4.98), and fentanyl (RR 2.26, 95% CI 1.34–3.82). In terms of hemodynamic safety, esketamine was superior to propofol (RR 5.24, 95% CI 2.48–11.09), sufentanil (RR 3.05, 95% CI 1.84–5.06), and fentanyl (RR 2.18, 95% CI 1.54–3.08) in preventing hypotension. Propofol was also associated with the highest risk of requiring vasoactive drugs (RR 7.17 versus esketamine). Regarding recovery, opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) significantly reduced PACU discharge time compared to esketamine (MD -4.96 min), whereas propofol and remifentanil prolonged it.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Esketamine exhibits a favorable safety profile in procedural sedation, characterized by superior hemodynamic stability and a reduced risk of respiratory depression compared to conventional opioids and propofol. These findings support its utility as a valuable component in balanced sedation and opioid-sparing protocols, particularly for patients at risk of hemodynamic instability.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Procedural sedation is a cornerstone of modern anesthesia practice and supports a wide range of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions including endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and minor surgical procedures [1]. The ideal sedative agent provides rapid onset, reliable efficacy, and rapid recovery while maintaining hemodynamic stability and preserving protective airway reflexes. Traditional agents such as propofol, midazolam, opioids including Sufentanil, fentanyl, and Remifentanil, and Dezocine remain central in practice. Their use is limited by dose-dependent respiratory depression, hemodynamic instability, and prolonged recovery times that affect patient safety and workflow efficiency [2–4].

Esketamine, the S-enantiomer of ketamine, has emerged as a potential alternative because of its distinctive pharmacological profile. As the more potent enantiomer at the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, Esketamine provides approximately twice the analgesic and anesthetic potency of racemic ketamine, which may allow for lower dosing and a potentially improved side-effect profile [5]. Compared to racemic ketamine, Esketamine exhibits approximately twice the analgesic and anesthetic potency while demonstrating a reduced incidence of psychotomimetic effects such as hallucinations and emergence delirium, making it particularly suitable for procedural sedation [5, 6]. In clinical practice, Esketamine is commonly administered intravenously as a bolus (typically 0.2–0.5 mg/kg) or as a continuous infusion, often in combination with other sedatives like propofol or midazolam to optimize sedation quality and minimize adverse effects [7, 8]. The doses employed in the included studies generally fall within this subanesthetic range, which may explain the favorable safety profile observed in terms of respiratory and hemodynamic stability. Recent evidence supports these advantages, as shown by a meta-analysis of 18 randomized controlled trials that reported improved subjective recovery in the first two postoperative days, reduced pain, and lower anxiety and depression scores with perioperative Esketamine, without a corresponding rise in adverse events [6]. A systematic review also reported neuroprotective effects, including a lower risk of postoperative delirium and delayed neurocognitive recovery within seven days after surgery [7]. During anesthetic induction, Esketamine reduced the incidence of opioid-induced cough by 70% compared with placebo while maintaining hemodynamic stability [8]. In the specific context of gastrointestinal endoscopy, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 trials demonstrated that Esketamine as an adjunct to propofol reduced recovery time and propofol dosage while decreasing hypotension and respiratory depression, though it increased visual disturbances [9].

The safety profile of Esketamine during procedural sedation remains unclear. Existing evidence is scattered across varied clinical settings, populations, comparators, and dosing strategies, with marked heterogeneity in outcome reporting [6–8]. Traditional meta-analyses have evaluated Esketamine against individual agents, yet comprehensive comparative data across the full range of available sedatives are limited. A network meta-analysis evaluating 37 pharmacological regimens for gastrointestinal endoscopy sedation found that while Esketamine-remimazolam demonstrated superior hemodynamic stability and faster recovery, no regimen outperformed propofol-opioids in sedation success, and comparative safety rankings across all sedatives remained uncertain [10]. This limits the ability to establish definitive comparative safety rankings and makes clinical decision making more difficult. Uncertainty persists regarding its relative safety in respiratory, hemodynamic, and psychotomimetic domains. This uncertainty extends to neuropsychiatric effects; for instance, a meta-analysis of cesarean delivery patients reported increased intraoperative hallucinations and dizziness with Esketamine, highlighting the need for sedation-specific safety data [11].

This study synthesizes available evidence through a systematic review and network meta-analysis to assess how Esketamine compares with commonly used sedatives in procedural settings. The main goal was to map and rank adverse event risks including respiratory depression, hemodynamic changes, airway issues, and recovery metrics. Additional aims included exploring how procedure type, Esketamine dose, and patient age may shape these safety outcomes.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This network meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Network Meta-Analyses (PRISMA-NMA) guideline [12]. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251245251). Registration was submitted on 02 December 2025, after the search phase began (04 November 2025) but prior to data extraction and synthesis. All outcomes and analytical plans were pre-specified in the protocol before data analysis to minimize the risk of selective reporting and post hoc decision-making.

sec.title: Search strategy and data sources
sec.p: A systematic search was conducted from database inception until October 2025 in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science using keywords and Medical Subject Headings for Esketamine, Procedural Sedation, Adverse Events, and Randomized Controlled Trial. Study selection was managed using Rayyan software [13], and the complete search strategies are provided in Supplementary Table 1. The initial search applied no language or date restrictions, and the final analysis included English-language studies published from 2000 onwards.

sec.title: Selection criteria
sec.p: Eligible participants were patients undergoing procedural sedation or monitored anesthesia care (MAC) for minimally invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedures. The intervention of interest was Esketamine in any dose or route, whether used alone or in combination. Comparator groups included other sedatives or analgesics such as propofol, midazolam, fentanyl, Sufentanil, Remifentanil, Dezocine, or placebo. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were eligible for inclusion in the quantitative network meta-analysis. Non-randomized studies were excluded from the pooled analysis to maintain methodological consistency and avoid potential bias from differing study designs. Case reports, non-human studies, and studies evaluating Esketamine for primary psychiatric treatment were excluded.

sec.title: Categorization of interventions and combination therapies
sec.p: Or the purposes of the network meta-analysis, intervention arms were grouped into distinct nodes according to the primary sedative or analgesic regimen administered. Treatment arms using a single pharmacological agent, such as esketamine alone, propofol alone, or sufentanil alone, were classified under the corresponding individual drug node. In contrast, arms employing a fixed-dose combination of two or more agents from different pharmacological classes were analyzed as separate, combination-specific nodes. For example, the regimen esketamine plus propofol was treated as a distinct intervention node and was not merged with either the esketamine or propofol monotherapy nodes. This approach preserves the unique pharmacodynamic interactions inherent to combination regimens and enables both direct and indirect comparisons with other single-agent and combination strategies within the network.

This categorization strategy ensures that the estimated treatment effect for each node accurately reflects the specific regimen evaluated. It also mitigates the risk of bias that would result from pooling combination therapies with their individual components, as the safety and efficacy profiles of combination regimens are not interchangeable with those of monotherapy. The resulting network geometry, presented in the Results section (Sect. " Discussion"), visually illustrates these distinct nodes and their interconnections.

In the current analysis, Esketamine was frequently administered as an adjunct rather than as a standalone agent. Consequently, the “Esketamine” node primarily represents studies in which esketamine was used as the sole or primary sedative or analgesic. Studies evaluating the combined esketamine–propofol regimen were assigned to a separate “Esketamine + Propofol” node, allowing for a clear distinction between esketamine monotherapy and combination therapy. This structure permits the evaluation of two clinically relevant questions: the comparative performance of esketamine alone versus other agents, and the performance of the specific esketamine–propofol combination versus alternative sedation regimens.

sec.title: Outcomes of interest included
sec.p: The primary safety outcomes included respiratory events such as hypoxia or desaturation, hemodynamic events such as hypotension, and bradycardia. Secondary safety outcomes included recovery parameters such as post anesthesia care unit discharge time.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: Two independent reviewers screened titles, abstracts, and full-text articles. Data extraction was performed using a standardized Excel sheet, piloted prior to use. Extracted information included study characteristics, patient demographics, procedural details, intervention and comparator regimens (drug, dose, route), and outcome data. Risk of bias for randomized controlled trials was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [14].

sec.title: Data synthesis and statistical analysis
sec.p: For outcomes with sufficient direct comparisons, pairwise meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model, with heterogeneity assessed via the I2 statistic [15], with values of 25%, 50%, and 75% considered to represent low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. The between-study variance was estimated using the Tau2 (τ2) statistic. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) [16]. A frequentist network meta-analysis was performed in R using the netmeta package [17], applying a random-effects model assuming a common heterogeneity variance, and the network geometry was plotted to visualize the evidence base. The transitivity assumption was evaluated by comparing clinical and methodological variables across treatment comparisons [18], while global inconsistency was assessed using the design-by-treatment interaction model [19] and local inconsistency using the side-splitting method [20]. Treatment rankings were estimated using Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) values and mean ranks, with higher SUCRA values indicating a more favorable safety profile [21].

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: A systematic literature search was performed using four electronic databases: PubMed (n = 126), Cochrane (n = 31), Scopus (n = 28), and Web of Science (n = 14), yielding 199 total records. After removal of 38 duplicate records, 161 unique records were screened by title and abstract. Following this initial screening, 90 records were excluded as they did not meet the inclusion criteria. Full-text retrieval was attempted for the remaining 71 articles, of which 18 were not accessible. Consequently, 53 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 29 reports were excluded for the following reasons: protocol publication (n = 1), clinical trials with no reported results (n = 14), non-qualifying language (n = 3), and high/moderate invasiveness (n = 11). A total of 39 studies were included in the final review. The study selection process is illustrated in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 1), and the complete search strategies are detailed in Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: Characteristics of included studies
sec.p: A total of 39 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. All were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), involving a combined total of 5,885 participants. Table 1 summarizes the key study characteristics, including design, country of origin, sample size, interventions, comparators, primary outcomes, and main findings. Geographically, most studies (n = 36) were conducted in China, with one study each originating from Germany, the Netherlands, and Taiwan.

sec.p: The clinical settings for esketamine administration were diverse, spanning a wide range of minimally invasive procedures and surgical interventions. These included diagnostic and therapeutic endoscopic procedures (e.g., gastrointestinal endoscopy, endoscopic ultrasound, bronchoscopy), gynecological surgeries (e.g., hysteroscopy and laparoscopic procedures), urological surgeries, thoracic surgery, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and orthopedic procedures such as shoulder arthroscopy.

Table 2 further details the intervention protocols. Esketamine was administered using various routes and regimens, including intravenous (IV) bolus, continuous IV infusion, patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA), and intranasal delivery. Comparators included active controls (e.g., sufentanil, fentanyl, alfentanil, dezocine, and remifentanil) or passive controls (normal saline placebo). As summarized in Table 1, reported outcomes focused on intraoperative parameters (e.g., hemodynamic stability and anesthetic or analgesic consumption), postoperative recovery (e.g., pain scores, opioid consumption, quality-of-recovery scores, and time to discharge), and safety outcomes (e.g., incidence of respiratory depression, hypotension, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and other adverse events).

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: The risk of bias was assessed for the 39 included studies across the five standard domains (D1–D5). A visual summary of the risk-of-bias distribution is presented in Fig. 2.

caption.p: Risk of bias assessment. The left panel displays a "traffic light" plot showing the authors' judgments for each included study across five domains (D1–D5). The right panel presents the aggregate risk of bias graph, illustrating the percentage of studies classified as low risk (green), some concerns (yellow), or high risk (red) for each domain and overall

sec.p: Overall, the methodological quality of the included studies was variable. As shown in the summary plot, 16 studies (41.0%) were judged to have an overall low risk of bias. The majority of studies (n = 21, 53.8%) were classified as having some concerns, while a small proportion (n = 2, 5.1%) were assessed as being at high risk of bias.

Across individual domains, the measurement of the outcome (D4) and the selection of the reported result (D5) demonstrated the highest methodological rigor. In both domains, 87.2% (n = 34) of studies were rated as low risk, with the remaining 12.8% (n = 5) categorized as having some concerns. No studies were judged to be at high risk in either domain.

sec.title: Network geometry
sec.p: Network plots were constructed for all primary and secondary outcomes, with a focus on interventions relevant to minimally invasive procedures. The geometries for the key respiratory and hemodynamic safety outcomes are presented below, while the remaining network plots are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

The network for hypoxia or desaturation (Fig. 3) demonstrated the most extensive geometry. Fentanyl, sufentanil, remifentanil, and propofol formed a dense core of direct comparisons. The opioid-free anesthesia strategy and esketamine were integrated into this network, enabling indirect comparisons with conventional opioid-based regimens.

caption.p: Network Geometry for Hypoxia in minimally invasive procedures

sec.p: For required airway interventions (Fig. 4), the network exhibited an intermediate structure. It incorporated a broad range of interventions, including regional anesthesia, a node not present in the respiratory depression networks. Connections among opioid-based anesthetics, the opioid-free anesthesia strategy, Esketamine, and propofol supported comparative analyses, although most comparisons were informed by a limited number of studies.

caption.p: Network Geometry for Required Airway Interventions in minimally invasive procedures

sec.p: The hemodynamic outcomes, including hypotension, vasoactive drug use, and bradycardia, were evaluated within comprehensive networks (Supplementary Figures S1 to S3). These networks featured frequent direct comparisons involving propofol, multiple opioids, and esketamine.

Recovery outcomes, including time to extubation, PACU discharge time, rescue analgesic use, and total propofol dose, were also well represented within the evidence network (Supplementary Figures S4 to S7). The network geometries were sufficiently connected to allow for robust mixed treatment comparisons.

sec.title: Description of nodes and edges
sec.p: The network plots for both primary and secondary outcomes predominantly showed a star-shaped topology. Across all networks—including hypotension, bradycardia, vasoactive drug use, time to extubation, PACU discharge time, total propofol dose, and respiratory adverse events—esketamine consistently occupied the central hub, serving as the common comparator and contributing the largest cumulative sample size.

Peripheral nodes represented various control and active comparators, most commonly placebo, propofol, and opioid-based regimens (sufentanil, fentanyl, remifentanil, dezocine, and grouped “other opioids”). Some interventions appeared only in outcome-specific networks; for example, dexmedetomidine was included in the bradycardia network, regional anesthesia in networks assessing vasoactive drug use, time to extubation, propofol dose, and airway interventions, and opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) in networks evaluating hypotension, bradycardia, time to extubation, hypoxia, and airway interventions.

Direct comparisons were largely concentrated between esketamine and individual comparators, with the most robust evidence for esketamine versus sufentanil and placebo. In contrast, direct head-to-head comparisons between peripheral interventions were limited or absent in several networks, indicating that relative effect estimates among these treatments were derived primarily from indirect evidence through the esketamine comparator.

sec.title: Primary outcomes: hypoxia
sec.p: The network meta-analysis for hypoxia demonstrated substantial variability in the relative effects of the included interventions when compared with esketamine. Across the network, Relative to esketamine, remifentanil exhibited a marked, though non-significant, increase in the risk of hypoxia (RR > 15.00, 95% CI 0.83–270.03; p = 0.066), achieving the highest SUCRA score (0.89). Propofol was associated with a significantly elevated risk (RR 6.11, 95% CI 1.91–19.57; p = 0.002), ranking second (SUCRA 0.86). Similarly, sufentanil (RR 2.72, 95% CI 1.48–4.98; p = 0.001), placebo (RR 2.34, 95% CI 1.03–5.32; p = 0.042), and fentanyl (RR 2.26, 95% CI 1.34–3.82; p = 0.002) all demonstrated statistically significant increases in hypoxia risk. No significant differences were observed for other opioids or opioid-free analgesia (OFA) versus esketamine (Fig. 5).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for hypoxia in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Required airway interventions
sec.p: Propofol demonstrated the highest point estimate for the risk of requiring airway interventions (RR 3.67, 95% CI 0.98 to 13.73), followed by placebo (RR 2.60, 95% CI 0.69 to 9.86). Fentanyl and sufentanil also showed elevated point estimates, although their confidence intervals were wide and overlapped unity. In contrast, opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) was associated with the lowest point estimate (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.89), suggesting a lower likelihood of airway intervention compared with esketamine, though this difference was not statistically significant. The SUCRA rankings were consistent with these patterns, with propofol demonstrating the highest probability of being associated with increased airway intervention requirements (SUCRA 0.84), whereas OFA ranked lowest (SUCRA 0.14). However, none of the comparisons reached statistical significance at the conventional threshold of p < 0.05, reflecting substantial uncertainty in the estimated effects (Fig. 6).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for required airway interventions in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Hypotension
sec.p: Esketamine was associated with a significantly lower risk of hypotension compared with most alternative interventions. The highest relative risk was observed with propofol (RR 5.24, 95% CI 2.48 to 11.09, p < 0.0001), which also ranked highest in the SUCRA analysis (0.92), indicating the greatest probability of hypotension among the evaluated treatments. Similarly, sufentanil (RR 3.05, 95% CI 1.84 to 5.06, p < 0.0001), placebo (RR 2.73, 95% CI 1.74 to 4.27, p < 0.0001), other opioids (RR 2.42, 95% CI 1.41 to 4.17, p = 0.0014), and fentanyl (RR 2.18, 95% CI 1.54 to 3.08, p < 0.0001) were all associated with significantly higher risks of hypotension relative to esketamine. In contrast, no statistically significant differences were observed between esketamine and either dezocine (RR 3.59, 95% CI 0.77 to 16.67, p = 0.1034) or opioid-free anesthesia (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.44, p = 0.7252); however, the wide confidence interval for dezocine indicates substantial imprecision and uncertainty in its effect estimate (Fig. 7).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for hypotension in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Bradycardia
sec.p: Fentanyl demonstrated the highest point estimate for the risk of bradycardia relative to esketamine (RR 8.06), although this association did not reach statistical significance (95% CI 0.90 to 71.89, p = 0.0615). In contrast, sufentanil was associated with a statistically significant increase in bradycardia risk compared with esketamine (RR 2.72, 95% CI 1.46 to 5.04, p = 0.0015). No other interventions, including dezocine, propofol, placebo, opioid-free anesthesia, or other opioids, demonstrated statistically significant differences in bradycardia risk relative to esketamine. The SUCRA rankings supported these findings, with fentanyl showing the highest probability of being the least favorable intervention for bradycardia (SUCRA 0.87), followed by dezocine (0.73) and sufentanil (0.72), whereas opioid-free anesthesia and other opioids ranked lowest for this outcome (Fig. 8).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for bradycardia in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Vasoactive drug use
sec.p: Compared to esketamine, propofol was associated with a significantly increased risk of vasoactive drug use (RR 7.17, 95% CI 2.80–18.36, p < 0.0001), ranking highest in SUCRA (1.00). Sufentanil (RR 2.26, 95% CI 1.64–3.11, p < 0.0001; SUCRA 0.82) and fentanyl (RR 1.96, 95% CI 1.40–2.73, p < 0.0001; SUCRA 0.74) also demonstrated increased risk, though to a lesser extent. Conversely, no statistically significant differences were observed when comparing esketamine to regional anesthesia (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.94–1.08, p = 0.914; SUCRA 0.36), placebo (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.95–1.06, p = 0.881; SUCRA 0.36), opioid-free anesthesia (OFA; RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.35–1.89, p = 0.630; SUCRA 0.22), or other opioids (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.19–1.99, p = 0.416; SUCRA 0.16) (Fig. 9).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for vasoactive drug use in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Secondary Outcomes: Time to extubation
sec.p: No treatment achieved a statistically significant difference in time to extubation relative to esketamine (all p > 0.05). Sufentanil exhibited the highest numerical trend toward prolonged extubation time (MD 1.58 min, 95% CI −0.74 to 3.91; SUCRA 0.79), whereas butorphanol showed the greatest trend toward reduced time (MD −1.00 min, 95% CI −4.71 to 2.71; SUCRA 0.26). Intermediate rankings were observed for placebo (SUCRA 0.64), propofol (SUCRA 0.61), other opioids (SUCRA 0.48), and fentanyl (SUCRA 0.33) (Fig. 10).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for time to extubation in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Total propofol dose
sec.p: Esketamine was associated with a statistically significant reduction in total propofol dose compared to placebo (MD 35.43, 95% CI 3.88 to 66.98, p = 0.0277). Conversely, no statistically significant differences were observed when comparing esketamine to various opioid interventions, including sufentanil (MD 17.12, 95% CI −5.83 to 40.08), remifentanil (MD 19.00, 95% CI −34.10 to 72.10), dezocine (MD 0.68, 95% CI −50.06 to 51.42), fentanyl (MD −2.28, 95% CI −30.98 to 26.41), or other opioids (MD −2.02, 95% CI −40.79 to 36.74). SUCRA analysis indicated that placebo was associated with the highest total propofol consumption (SUCRA 0.88), followed by sufentanil (0.67) and remifentanil (0.63), while fentanyl presented the lowest likelihood of increased consumption (SUCRA 0.29) (Fig. 11).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for total propofol dose in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) discharge time
sec.p: Opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) was the only intervention associated with a statistically significant reduction in discharge time compared to esketamine (MD −4.96 min, 95% CI −9.07 to −0.84, p = 0.0183). Conversely, both remifentanil (MD 9.30 min, 95% CI 3.66 to 14.94, p = 0.0012) and propofol (MD 6.60 min, 95% CI 2.53 to 10.67, p = 0.0015) resulted in significantly prolonged PACU discharge times relative to the reference group, while no significant differences were observed for fentanyl, sufentanil, other opioids, or placebo. Consistently, SUCRA rankings identified remifentanil (0.96) and propofol (0.89) as having the highest probability of prolonged discharge, whereas OFA (0.01) ranked as the most effective intervention for minimizing the duration of stay (Fig. 12).

caption.p: Forest plot of network meta-analysis for PACU discharge time in minimally invasive procedures

sec.title: Rescue analgesic use
sec.p: No statistically significant differences were observed between esketamine and any of the comparator interventions regarding rescue analgesic use, as all 95% confidence intervals crossed the line of no effect. Despite the lack of significance, sufentanil exhibited the strongest trend toward increased use (RR 2.38, 95% CI 0.85–6.68) and ranked highest in SUCRA (0.88). Placebo (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.71–1.95; SUCRA 0.51) and remifentanil (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.30–4.55; SUCRA 0.49) displayed risk profiles similar to the reference. Conversely, other opioids showed a non-significant trend toward lower use (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.24–2.87), ranking lowest in probability of rescue analgesic requirements (SUCRA 0.29) (Fig. 13).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA), comprising 39 randomized controlled trials and 5,885 participants, provides a comprehensive synthesis of the comparative safety and efficacy of esketamine in procedural sedation and analgesia (PSA). Our findings indicate that esketamine-based strategies, particularly when used within an opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) or opioid-sparing regimen, offer distinct advantages in maintaining hemodynamic stability and reducing recovery times compared with conventional opioid-based sedation. Specifically, esketamine was associated with a significantly lower risk of hypotension and reduced vasoactive drug requirement compared with propofol and sufentanil. While respiratory safety profiles were generally comparable across opioid regimens, propofol monotherapy was associated with the highest risk of hypoxia and airway interventions.

The principal finding of this NMA is the superior hemodynamic stability associated with esketamine. Propofol and sufentanil demonstrated significantly higher risks of hypotension and vasoactive drug use compared with esketamine. These findings are consistent with recent randomized trials. Feng et al. reported that low-dose esketamine combined with propofol resulted in more stable mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate trends, along with reduced vasoactive drug use, compared with sufentanil-propofol regimens in elderly patients undergoing bronchoscopy [24]. Similarly, Guan et al. observed significantly lower intraoperative blood pressure fluctuations and reduced vasoactive medication requirements in patients receiving esketamine during hysteroscopic surgery [25].

Evidence from studies included in our analysis further reinforces these findings. Zhao et al. demonstrated that patients receiving esketamine during tracheoscopic drug injection maintained higher and more stable blood pressure compared with those receiving sufentanil, who experienced significant MAP reductions after anesthesia induction [59]. Zhao et al. similarly reported that both low-dose and high-dose esketamine significantly attenuated decreases in MAP and heart rate during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, preventing hypotension observed in saline controls [58]. Zhao et al. (2025) showed that combining esketamine with remimazolam during gastroscopy resulted in more stable hemodynamics and a lower incidence of hypotension compared with remimazolam alone, supporting the role of esketamine’s sympathomimetic properties in counteracting sedative-induced cardiovascular depression [60].

Additional validation comes from Zhang et al., who reported significantly lower intraoperative norepinephrine requirements in patients receiving esketamine during thoracic surgery compared with controls [55]. Zhang et al. further demonstrated that esketamine reduced the incidence of cardio-biliary reflex during laparoscopic cholecystectomy [56]. Xue et al. (2025) reported lower hypotension rates in high-altitude patients undergoing gastroscopy with esketamine-propofol compared with fentanyl-propofol regimens [61], while Xu et al. (2022) observed smaller MAP reductions with esketamine compared with dezocine during gastroscopy [50]. However, Yan et al. highlighted an important nuance in thoracoscopic surgery, where patients receiving esketamine-based OFA required higher esmolol doses to manage sympathetic responses during intubation [53]. These findings indicate that while esketamine effectively prevents hypotension, its sympathomimetic effects may require modulation during highly stimulating procedures. Overall, the consistency of evidence supports esketamine as a preferable agent for patients at risk of hemodynamic instability.

Respiratory safety remains a critical concern in PSA. Our NMA showed that propofol monotherapy carried the highest probability of hypoxia and airway intervention, whereas esketamine and OFA regimens ranked lowest for hypoxia risk. These results are supported by Zhao et al., who reported no respiratory depression events in esketamine-treated patients compared with a 13.33% incidence in controls [58]. Zhao et al. similarly observed stable oxygen saturation with esketamine and no significant respiratory adverse events [59]. Wang et al. demonstrated lower transient hypoxemia rates in pediatric patients receiving propofol-esketamine compared with propofol-fentanyl [62].

In obese patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy, Zhang et al. reported significantly lower rates of severe hypoxemia with remimazolam-esketamine compared with propofol-esketamine, suggesting that esketamine’s respiratory-sparing effects may be optimized when combined with non-propofol sedatives in high-risk populations [54]. Xue et al. provided further evidence from high-altitude settings, where hypoxemia rates were significantly lower with esketamine than with fentanyl [61]. Although Xu et al. found no statistically significant difference in desaturation events between esketamine and dezocine, the absolute number of events favored esketamine [50]. Collectively, these findings support the preservation of spontaneous respiration as a key safety advantage of esketamine.

The propofol-sparing effect of esketamine was significant in our NMA compared with placebo. This finding aligns with Zhao et al., who demonstrated reduced propofol and opioid consumption in both low-dose and high-dose esketamine groups [58]. Zhao et al. further showed that esketamine reduced the effective dose of remimazolam required for gastroscopy in a dose-dependent manner [60]. However, some heterogeneity was observed. Zhao et al. found no significant difference in propofol consumption between esketamine and sufentanil during tracheoscopy, likely reflecting procedural or protocol-specific factors [59].

Other studies consistently demonstrated reduced anesthetic and opioid requirements with esketamine. Xue et al. reported a 25.5% reduction in propofol dose [61], while Xu et al. observed lower propofol consumption with esketamine compared with dezocine [50]. Zhang et al. reported a marked reduction in sufentanil use during non-intubated thoracic surgery [55], and Wang et al. showed reduced postoperative opioid consumption in elderly patients [63]. These findings highlight esketamine’s robust opioid-sparing capacity, although its impact on total anesthetic dose may vary by surgical context.

Recovery profiles and quality of recovery are essential considerations. Our NMA identified OFA as the most effective strategy for reducing PACU discharge time, whereas propofol and remifentanil were associated with longer recovery. Zhao et al. reported faster awakening and shorter recovery times with esketamine compared with opioid-based regimens [58, 59]. In contrast, Zhao et al. (2025) found prolonged recovery when esketamine was added to remimazolam, which was attributed to esketamine’s longer half-life relative to ultra-short-acting sedatives [60]. This underscores the importance of agent selection and context when interpreting recovery outcomes.

Several studies reported improved quality of recovery and postoperative outcomes with esketamine. Zhang et al. demonstrated higher QoR-40 scores, reduced pain intensity, and attenuation of hyperalgesia [55, 57]. Reduced postoperative nausea and vomiting were consistently observed across multiple studies, including Zhao et al. [58], Zhang et al. [55], and Xue et al. [51]. However, psychological outcomes varied. Wang et al. reported lower anxiety and depression scores but a higher incidence of dissociative symptoms, whereas other trials found no significant differences in hallucinations or delirium [63]. These findings suggest that age, dosage, and procedural context influence the psychotomimetic profile of esketamine.

This study has limitations inherent to the network meta-analytic design. First, The included trials varied widely in surgical procedures and sedation protocols, which may contribute to heterogeneity. Second, although risk of bias was assessed, variability in randomization and reporting quality across studies warrants cautious interpretation. Additionally, psychotomimetic adverse events were inconsistently reported, limiting definitive conclusions regarding neuropsychiatric safety. Third, while racemic ketamine is a well-established agent in procedural sedation and analgesia, this review focused specifically on esketamine. This decision was driven by esketamine’s distinct pharmacological profile, including its higher receptor affinity and a differing adverse-effect spectrum, particularly with respect to psychotomimetic effects. In addition, the expanding clinical use of esketamine as a defined and independent agent justified a dedicated comparative safety evaluation. Pooling studies of racemic ketamine and esketamine would introduce substantial clinical and pharmacological heterogeneity, which could violate the transitivity assumption required for a valid network meta-analysis and obscure agent-specific safety inferences. Consequently, the comparative safety of esketamine versus racemic ketamine remains an important topic for future direct investigation. Fourth, although we initially planned a subgroup analysis to explore the dose-dependent safety effects of esketamine (using a threshold of 0.3 mg/kg), this analysis could not be conducted. The included studies reported dosing using disparate methods (e.g., fixed bolus doses, variable bolus plus infusion, total mg only), which precluded the consistent categorization of patients into low- and high-dose subgroups for reliable pooled comparison. Future studies should aim to standardize the reporting of weight-adjusted esketamine doses to facilitate robust dose–response evaluations. Fifth, the network was constrained by the availability of direct comparative evidence. Several emerging agents, most notably remimazolam, could not be included as independent comparators because of insufficient head-to-head data with esketamine in the included randomized trials. In addition, the use of pharmacological antagonists, such as flumazenil and naloxone, was not systematically evaluated, as the analysis focused on primary sedative regimens rather than reversal strategies. This limitation is particularly relevant for recovery outcomes, including time to extubation and PACU discharge, which may be substantially influenced by antagonist use. Variation and inconsistent reporting of antagonist administration across studies introduced an unadjustable confounding factor. Future trials should directly compare esketamine with newer agents and prospectively standardize and report antagonist use to enable more definitive assessments of comparative safety and recovery profiles.

This network meta-analysis demonstrates that esketamine, particularly within opioid-free or opioid-sparing regimens, offers a favorable safety and efficacy profile for procedural sedation. It provides superior hemodynamic stability, reduces vasoactive drug use, and lowers the risk of hypoxia compared with conventional opioid-based strategies. While its propofol-sparing and recovery effects are context-dependent, esketamine consistently reduces opioid-related adverse events such as postoperative nausea and pruritus, with an acceptable and generally transient risk of dissociative symptoms. These findings support esketamine as a valuable alternative to traditional opioids in patients undergoing minimally invasive procedures.
